issues.legal_issue: An accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt where the evidence establishes presence but does not establish an overt act connecting that accused to the fatal assault.
material_facts: The second accused was present with the other accused and carried a spade, but the evidence did not establish an overt act by him apart from his presence.
The prosecution attributed an instigating statement to him, but a witness whose committal-court evidence was admitted at trial did not give evidence of that instigation.
The eldest brother inflicted the fatal injury, and the Court considered it unlikely that he needed the second accused’s instigation.
issues.conclusion: The second accused was entitled to the benefit of doubt; his conviction and sentence were set aside and he was directed to be released.
issues.legal_principle: Where there is no legal evidence of an accused’s overt act connecting him to the offence, the benefit of doubt must follow. Considering the evidence and probabilities, the Court found the alleged instigation unlikely and insufficient to sustain the conviction.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_against_conviction and accused_presence_established and not_evidence_of_overt_act and alleged_instigation_unlikely

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: The case is an appeal by an accused challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.accused_presence_established: The evidence establishes that the accused was present at the scene with others involved in the incident.
predicates.not_evidence_of_overt_act: The evidence does not establish an overt act by the accused connecting that person to the offence.
predicates.alleged_instigation_unlikely: The circumstances and evidence make it unlikely that the accused’s alleged instigation caused or prompted the fatal act.

issues.definition: When a convicted accused’s presence is established but no overt act is proved and the alleged instigation is unlikely, the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt.

issues.legal_issue: Prior testimony from a committal proceeding may be treated as evidence at trial when it is read to the witness in full and the witness admits making it, without confronting the witness passage by passage.
material_facts: At trial, the witnesses gave versions contrary to their evidence in the committal proceeding.
The prior testimony was read to the witnesses in full, and they admitted that they had given and signed it.
The prior testimony was transferred to the trial record and treated as evidence.
issues.conclusion: The procedure complied with the requirements for treating the prior testimony as evidence, and the challenge to its admissibility failed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 288 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, prior committal evidence may be treated as evidence at trial, subject to the Evidence Act. The Court held that reading the statements in extenso and obtaining the witnesses’ admission that they made them complied with section 145 of the Evidence Act, 1872. It considered Tara Singh v. State of Punjab, Bhagwan Singh v. State of Punjab, and State of Rajasthan v. Kartar Singh; the admission of the prior statement distinguished the circumstances from those in Tara Singh.

predicates.criminal_trial_using_prior_committal_tes: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which testimony given by a witness in an earlier committal proceeding is sought to be used as evidence.
predicates.prior_testimony_read_in_full: The witness’s earlier testimony is read to the witness in full.
predicates.witness_admits_making_prior_testimony: The witness admits having made the earlier testimony.

issues.definition: In a criminal trial using earlier committal testimony, reading it in full and obtaining the witness’s admission that it was made permits it to be treated as trial evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s statement recorded by a magistrate during an investigation is not tainted merely because it was recorded to guard against the possibility that the witness might be influenced, and it may corroborate the witness’s committal-court testimony.
material_facts: During the investigation, the police arranged for statements of witnesses to be recorded by a magistrate because they feared the witnesses might be gained over.
The witnesses supported the prosecution in the committal proceeding but resiled from that testimony at trial.
The High Court relied on the magistrate-recorded statements to corroborate the witnesses’ committal-court testimony.
issues.conclusion: The magistrate-recorded statements were not tainted merely because they had been obtained as a precaution against the witnesses being gained over, and they could corroborate the witnesses’ committal-court testimony.
issues.legal_principle: Section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, does not make a witness’s evidence tainted merely because the police arranged for a magistrate to record the witness’s statement out of concern that the witness might be gained over. The court must assess credibility in light of all the circumstances, including any later change in testimony. Under section 157 of the Evidence Act, 1872, such a statement may corroborate testimony given in the committal proceeding, though the recorded statement is not itself evidence. The Court relied on Ram Chandra v. State of U.P. and State of Rajasthan v. Kartar Singh.

predicates.criminal_trial_assessing_prior_witness_s: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which a witness’s earlier statements and testimony are considered.
predicates.magistrate_recorded_statement_during_inv: A witness made a statement recorded by a magistrate during the investigation.
predicates.statement_recorded_as_precaution_against: The statement was recorded because investigators were concerned that the witness might be influenced or induced to change their account.
predicates.witness_gave_committal_testimony: The witness gave testimony in an earlier committal proceeding.

issues.definition: In a criminal trial, a magistrate-recorded statement made during an investigation as a precaution against witness influence is not tainted for that reason alone and may corroborate the witness’s committal testimony.

issues.legal_issue: One witness’s testimony from a committal proceeding, when admitted as evidence at trial, may corroborate another witness’s such testimony.
material_facts: The prosecution relied on the committal-court testimony of several witnesses after they resiled from that testimony at trial.
The witnesses’ committal-court testimony was admitted as evidence at trial.
The High Court treated the testimony of one witness as corroborating that of another.
issues.conclusion: There was no flaw in treating one witness’s admitted committal-court testimony as corroborative of another’s.
issues.legal_principle: Testimony admitted under section 288 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, is treated as substantive evidence in law. The Court therefore held that the admitted testimony of one witness could corroborate the admitted testimony of another.

predicates.criminal_trial_with_multiple_admitted_co: The proceeding is a criminal trial in which testimony from a committal proceeding by more than one witness is relied on.
predicates.each_testimony_treated_as_trial_evidence: The committal testimony of each witness has been admitted and treated as evidence at trial.

issues.definition: In a criminal trial, when the committal testimony of multiple witnesses is admitted as evidence, one witness’s testimony may corroborate another’s.
